name: Luxembourg
headline: Every insured person gets a shared record with an access log and blocking tools, but few patients activate it and the EU says access lags.

access.summary: The 2014 patient rights law gives a right to a full copy within 15 working days, and a national shared record holds lab, imaging and discharge reports. Patients activate only about 3,257 accounts a month, and the EU rates record access as lagging.
detail: Article 16 of the law of 24 July 2014 gives the patient access to the patient file and all health information. A copy, on paper or digital, must be supplied within 15 working days, and the fee cannot exceed the cost of copying and sending.
Providers must keep the file for at least ten years after care ends (Article 15).
The Agence eSanté creates a shared care record (DSP) automatically for everyone insured. It holds lab reports, imaging reports, hospital discharge letters and care summaries (Guichet.lu, May 2026).
By end 2025 the DSP held 18.3 million documents in 1.2 million open records. Patients activated 3,257 accounts a month on average and opened 166,394 documents a month (Le Quotidien, July 2026).
The European Commission's 2026 country report says eHealth is below the EU average and electronic record access is lagging.

control.summary: The patient can oppose sharing at any time, close the record, block named professionals or mask data, and see a log of every access. The record is created by default, and the referring doctor cannot be blocked.
detail: Article 60quater of the Social Security Code gives a right to see the record, a right to know who accessed it, and a right to oppose sharing at any time.

The Grand-Ducal Regulation of 6 December 2019 sets a default access matrix by profession. Patients can set a professional to a private level (blocked) or a restricted level (some data masked) (Article 6).
Every access and action is traced and kept, and the patient can consult the access history (Article 8).
The record is opened automatically on affiliation, so the default is opt-out. Patients can deny access to any professional except their referring doctor (Guichet.lu).
Since 1 December 2025 patients can activate their account through MyGuichet.lu and name a trusted helper to manage it (Ministry of Health).

privacy.summary: Luxembourg applies the GDPR through its law of 1 August 2018, but the regulator's published decisions we reviewed show no health-sector case. An August 2026 attack on an IT provider cut at least 80 medical practices off from patient files.
detail: Health data is a special category under the GDPR. The law of 1 August 2018 organises the national regulator (CNPD) and lets it fine controllers, but not the State or municipalities.
The CNPD's published decisions cover video surveillance, registers and data officers. None of those we reviewed involve a hospital, doctor, lab or insurer, so this score rests on the general law.

On 22 August 2026 a cyberattack hit BMS Engineering, which hosts eMed software for doctors. At least 80 practices lost access to records for days, and a leak was not ruled out (L'essentiel, Reporter.lu).
Whether the breach was notified to the CNPD was not verified.

commercial.summary: National law bans processing genetic data for employment and insurance purposes, and only anonymised shared-record data may leave care for statistics. No Luxembourg ban on selling health data or on health advertising was verified, so the score stays low in its band.
detail: Article 66 of the law of 1 August 2018 prohibits processing genetic data to exercise an employer's or insurer's rights.

Shared-record access is limited to the referring doctor, the treating doctor and professionals taking part in care. Agencies may exchange only anonymised data for statistics or epidemiology (Article 60quater).
Rules on data brokers, consumer health apps and sale of de-identified data beyond the GDPR were not verified.

journey.summary: One national record collects hospital, lab and imaging documents, and professionals must upload useful data. National e-prescription use was not verified, and the EU tells Luxembourg to speed up its record rollout.
detail: The DSP is an interface, not a replacement for provider files. Professionals holding useful data must upload it within a reasonable time (Regulation of 6 December 2019).
It held 18.3 million documents by end 2025. The electronic vaccination booklet had 75,173 booklets and over 500,000 recorded vaccinations (Le Quotidien).
Nationwide e-prescription for medicines was not verified, so this score stays in the lower half of the mixed band.
Luxembourg exchanges patient summaries and e-prescriptions across EU borders. EHDS deadlines start March 2029, and a DigiSanté programme with 25 sub-projects began in October 2025.

clinical.summary: Treating professionals can open the shared record within a profession-based access matrix, unless the patient blocks them. Professionals opened only 34,129 documents a month in 2025, so clinical use is still small.
detail: Access is limited to the referring doctor, treating doctor and professionals in the patient's care (Article 60quater). A default matrix sets what each profession may read and write.
In an emergency, professionals see essential data only if the patient granted them access (Agence eSanté). A separate break-glass rule was not found in the regulation.
Professional document views rose 92.4% to 34,129 a month, against 166,394 by patients (Le Quotidien, July 2026).
The August 2026 attack showed many practices depend on hosted software outside the DSP.

research.summary: Trials need ministry approval after ethics committee review, and the data law requires pseudonymisation or similar safeguards for research. No general opt-out from secondary use exists yet, and the EHDS access body is still being prepared.
detail: Under Article 27 of the hospitals law of 18 March 2018, research on people needs ministerial authorisation after advice from the Health Directorate and the national research ethics committee (CNER).
Articles 64 and 65 of the law of 1 August 2018 require anonymisation, pseudonymisation or functional separation for research and statistics.
LNDS runs HDAB-LU, a four-year project from January 2024 to build the future health data access body. LNDS says the body itself will be designated by a future EHDS law.
We found no individual opt-out from secondary use of health data.

ai.summary: Clinical AI falls under EU device law and the EU AI Act only. Bill 8476, which would name national AI Act authorities, was still in committee after a State Council opinion of 10 July 2026.
detail: AI used as a medical device needs CE marking under the EU MDR and will face AI Act high-risk duties.
Bill 8476 was filed on 23 December 2024 to implement the AI Act. Parliament lists it as in committee, with no vote (Chambre des Députés).
The CNPD is set to take new AI Act tasks, but in January 2026 it described national governance as still being planned.
No national rules for AI in care were verified.

news.headline: Patients can now activate shared health record online through MyGuichet.lu
news.source: Ministère de la Santé et de la Sécurité sociale
news.why: Removes the wait for a posted code, a barrier to reading one's own record.

news.headline: Data regulator prepares for new AI Act supervision duties
news.why: Shows who may oversee AI systems, including in care, once the law passes.

news.headline: eSanté report shows shared record use rising but still modest
news.why: Patients and doctors open more documents, yet activations stay near 3,000 a month.

news.headline: EU report says Luxembourg lags on electronic health record access
